questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: I wanted to challenge myself, and I wanted to try something new for a semester.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: That they speak English so I could understand the locals. That the city seemed nice, and that there was a nice selection of courses.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was a bit difficult at times, but I think the people at KU-Abroad was very helpful!

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I didn't receive any really, I didn't need it:)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I could choose between shared bathrooms or en-suite, and catered or self-catered. It's mostly shared flats, I know a few that have their own flat, but mostly it's shared (the kitchen and bathroom). The flats are located all across town, and most of them are never more than like 30 minutes away from campus.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You could choose catered or self-catered, and I think catered is mostly Pollock Halls, which are known to have a quite posh reputation. My shared kitchen is fairly large and we are 7 people in the flat, with two stoves, two fridges/freezers and an oven. It was alright:)

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: If you are lucky you can get to stay with post-grad people that are a bit older, as a lot of the people that stay on campus are first year students, but from what I've heard the freshers are very social as they are new to town as well so you can go explore the city together. Even if you live with post-grad flatmates, that doesn't mean that they are more clean and better flatmates, just because they are older:) And the rooms you sign up for on the waitlist is probably not the one you get, as all the English and Scottish people get those, and us exchange people get the reaaaally expensive ones. But it's really nice that if something is broken or there's an issue with something, you have a legit "landlord" that will come and fix it, and you get a proper contract, so that's nice!

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was really lucky with the location of my accommodation and the facilities, however it was really expensive. I paid around 3.500£ for the semester, but it is just a really expensive city in terms of rent, I know a lot of people that have paid even more, but mostly it's around this much.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The courses I applied for weren't available, and then when we had to like apply a second time after we've been accepted the full course list wasn't available either so I just signed up for something and then I was just appointed to some courses that were at the bottom of my list, but then I could just apply for them to be changed when the course list was updated, but that wasn't until maybe the middle of august. But really nice that you can change course during the first two weeks of classes, I changed one of my courses in the first week and that was also really easy.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: There was a website that explained how to do it, and other than that I just emailed the uni a few times, and they were always quick to respond.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: In the end I got them, but it took some patience in waiting for the course list to be updated.  Even though there were some courses I really wanted that weren't available at my semester, which was really a bummer, there were some new courses that were cool.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Don't stress out about the courses that you apply with, they are probably a bit different when you have to sign up for them later, but there will probably still be some nice courses when the time comes.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took one year 2 course, one year 3 course and one year 4 course.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The lectures were quite similar. The tutorials is not something I've tried before, but it was really nice. We were around 6-12 people each time in my tutorials and then we just talked with a TA about the week's readings and themes, they were quite intense sometimes, especially when we weren't that many and the TA expects you to talk, but they didn't say anything if you said you didn't have anything to add, at least in my tutorials.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: Gender in the contemporary world, anthropology of displacement and migration, culture and power

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Anthropology of displacement and migration!!!! It was so good, and the professor Lucy Lowe is a great teacher!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Not really anything I can think of

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: The food shops are quite similar in price as Denmark, the bus is way cheaper than I thought, like 1-2£ for where ever you wanted to go.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There are so many clubs and societies it's crazy! There's a crochet and knit society, a winter swimming society, and a society that just go around testing chips in Edinburgh! And then a lot of sports, but they are a bit more clubs, at least some of them, where there's try outs and everything, not like KU-studenteridræt.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Definitely all of the erasmus stuff and the international events that the uni throws, it's a great way to meet other international people.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: The highlands! It's sooo beautiful! In Edinburgh you should just explore the city and go out where there aren't that many tourists and students, like out in Leith and down Easter Road, or Bruntsfield also really nice! And try get the train to Glasgow, it's a really cool city and very different from Edinburgh, but the people are really nice!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy, it felt very normal very quick. The fact that I can speak the same language as everyone is very nice, and it's just such a cosy city.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: No not really, I didn't really talk with a lot of local people, mostly international people. I think if I would have been more involved in some of the societies I probably would have talked more with some local students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: I can't really think of anything major. In the quiet areas of the library a lot of people still talk, a bit annoying, but that's it.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer:
I really like how all of the professors use microphones and give out microphones to the students when they have a question, that's really nice! Uhh and at cafés they really like cake, like not just all of the fancy pastries from the copenhagen bakeries, this is caaake, and it's really good. 
Generally people are very different and you see a lot of different ways to dress and act, and think that's really cool, compared to how Copenhagen sometimes can be a bit pretentious and take itself very serious, Edinburgh doesn't really do that, in a very nice way.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: The rent is really expensive! The city is really nice! The course list is really unreliable.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Even if you think you're english is good, some of the accents of the professors and TA's can be a bit challenging, but even the native speakers think that so.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Meeting new people:)

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: maybe the fact they you don't really get "læseferie" and they have midterms in the middle of the semester while you still have your courses to read for, so you don't have time to read in the middle of the semester and then a month later there's finals and because you haven't had time to read you have to read for your final while you also have courses.... But they have extensions where you can get 4-ish days extra to do your essays, so that's nice!

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
